title: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
summary: Fine-tune big models by training a small low-rank update: why full fine-tuning is costly, LoRA's math and parameter counts, merging, QLoRA's 4-bit NF4 base, other PEFT methods, and where LoRA falls short.
outcomes: Explain why full fine-tuning with Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter and what intrinsic dimension suggests
Compute LoRA's trainable parameter count for any rank and set of target matrices
Explain why B starts at zero, what alpha/r does, and why a merged LoRA adds no inference latency
Describe how QLoRA's NF4, double quantization and paged optimizers fit a 65B fine-tune on one GPU
Choose between LoRA, other PEFT methods and full fine-tuning given the task and forgetting risk

lessons.title: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be

blocks.md: Recall from the training course that **supervised fine-tuning** keeps training a pretrained model on task data, and in its plain form every weight receives a gradient and an update. This is **full fine-tuning**. It works, but for large models it has two costs that grow with parameter count: the GPU memory needed to train, and the storage and serving cost of one full model copy per task.

Start with training memory. With mixed-precision training and the Adam optimizer, each parameter needs a 16-bit weight (2 bytes) and a 16-bit gradient (2 bytes), plus optimizer state kept in 32-bit: a master copy of the weight, Adam's momentum and Adam's variance (4 bytes each). The ZeRO paper (Rajbhandari et al.) sums this to **16 bytes per parameter**, before counting activations.

blocks.title: Training memory for a 7B model with mixed-precision Adam

scenes.caption: Inference only: a Llama-2-7B-shaped model has 6.74B parameters, so 2 bytes each is 13.5 GB.
Backpropagation adds a gradient for every weight: another 13.5 GB.
Adam keeps three fp32 tensors per parameter (12 bytes): 80.9 GB. Total 107.8 GB, more than one 80 GB GPU holds, and activations are still extra.

blocks.md: Three quarters of that memory is optimizer state, and it exists only because every parameter is trainable. The second cost is storage: each fine-tune is a full copy. The LoRA paper's example is GPT-3 175B, where every task-specific copy is about 350 GB, so 100 tasks would need about 35 TB.

Is all that freedom needed? Aghajanyan, Zettlemoyer and Gupta (2020) measured the **intrinsic dimension** of fine-tuning, an idea from Li et al. (2018): the smallest number of free parameters that still solves the task well. They freeze the pretrained weights $\theta_0$ and train only a small vector $\theta^d$ that a fixed random projection $P$ maps into the full parameter space:

blocks.caption: Only the d entries of the small vector are trained. D is the full parameter count. Starting from a zero vector recovers the pretrained model exactly.

blocks.md: They call the smallest $d$ that reaches 90% of the full fine-tuning score $d_{90}$. On MRPC (a paraphrase task with about 3,700 training examples), RoBERTa-Large reaches that bar with only about 200 trained numbers, even though the model has 355M parameters.

blocks.title: Measured d90 on MRPC (structure-aware method, Table 1)

scenes.caption: Every model needs only hundreds to low thousands of free parameters to get 90% of the way to full fine-tuning on MRPC.
The larger model of each family has the lower intrinsic dimension (BERT-Large below BERT-Base, RoBERTa-Large lowest at 207). The paper reports this trend across more than a dozen models.

blocks.md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank, so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

A d90 of 200 does not mean that 200 hand-picked weights would do. The 200 numbers are projected through a dense random map, so every original weight still moves a little. And 90% of full performance is the bar, not 100%.

blocks.question: You fine-tune a 7B model with Adam but freeze all but 1% of its weights. Which part of the 107.8 GB shrinks the most?
options: The 16-bit copy of the frozen weights, because frozen weights are not loaded
Nothing changes, because Adam allocates state for every weight in the model
Gradients and Adam states, because they are only needed for trainable weights
Activations, because a frozen layer does not store activations
blocks.explain: Frozen weights still have to sit in memory for the forward pass, and activations are still needed to backpropagate into trainable parts. But gradients and the three fp32 optimizer tensors exist only for trainable parameters, so 14 of the 16 bytes per parameter disappear for the frozen 99%.

blocks.question: Aghajanyan et al. report d90 of about 200 for RoBERTa-Large on MRPC. What does this measure?
options: The number of training examples needed to reach 90% accuracy
The size of a random subspace in which training reaches 90% of full fine-tuning's score
The rank of RoBERTa-Large's weight matrices
The number of layers that must be fine-tuned
blocks.explain: d90 is the smallest dimension d of the trainable vector, projected randomly into the full parameter space, whose training reaches 90% of the full fine-tuning metric. It says nothing directly about data size or the rank of the pretrained weights.

lessons.title: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update

blocks.md: Take one dense layer with pretrained weight $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, computing $h = W_0 x$. Full fine-tuning learns a new matrix $W_0 + \Delta W$ with all $dk$ entries free. **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation, Hu et al. 2021) freezes $W_0$ and forces the update to be a product of two thin matrices: $\Delta W = BA$ with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$.

blocks.tex: h = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x
blocks.caption: The LoRA forward pass (Hu et al. Eq. 3 with the alpha over r scaling). W0 is frozen; only A and B are trained.

blocks.md: The **rank** $r$ is tiny compared with $d$ and $k$, often 1 to 64 against a few thousand. A product of a $d \times r$ and an $r \times k$ matrix has rank at most $r$, so the update can only push the layer's outputs along $r$ directions. The cost is $r(d+k)$ trainable numbers instead of $dk$. Note what is *not* low rank: $W_0$ itself stays full rank and untouched.

Here is a 4 by 4 example with $r = 1$ and $\alpha = 2$, so the scale $\alpha / r$ is 2. A is a 1 by 4 row, B is a 4 by 1 column, and their product is a full 4 by 4 matrix with only 8 free numbers behind it.

blocks.title: A rank-1 update on a 4 by 4 weight

scenes.caption: The pretrained weight W0. It is frozen: no gradient, no optimizer state.
The update (alpha/r)BA at initialization. B starts at zero, so the whole update is zero and the model behaves exactly like the pretrained one.
After training, A = [0.4, -0.1, 0.2, 0.3] and B = [0.5, 0, -0.25, 0.25]. Every row of 2BA is a multiple of A: 16 entries, 8 free numbers, rank 1.
Merged weight W0 + 2BA. Row 2 is unchanged because B's second entry is 0. This single matrix gives exactly the same outputs as computing the two paths separately.

blocks.title: The LoRA forward pass on x = [1, 2, 0, -1]
blocks.code:
def lora_forward(x, W0, A, B, alpha, r):
    base = W0 @ x          # frozen path
    z = A @ x              # shrink: k dims to r dims
    delta = B @ z          # expand: r dims to d dims
    return base + (alpha / r) * delta

h = lora_forward(x, W0, A, B, alpha=2, r=1)

scenes.caption: The frozen path is an ordinary matrix-vector product with W0.
A squeezes the 4-dim input into r = 1 number: 0.4(1) - 0.1(2) + 0.2(0) + 0.3(-1) = -0.1.
B spreads that one number back out to 4 outputs.
Scale by alpha/r = 2 and add. The result equals the merged weight times x from the matrix figure.

blocks.prompt: At the very first training step, B is zero and A is random. Which of the two matrices receives a nonzero gradient?
blocks.reveal: Only **B**. With upstream gradient $g = \partial L / \partial h$, the gradients are $\partial L/\partial B = s\, g (Ax)^\top$ and $\partial L/\partial A = s\, B^\top g\, x^\top$, where $s = \alpha/r$. Since $B = 0$, A's gradient is zero, while B's is not because $Ax$ is nonzero for a random A. After one step B is nonzero and both matrices learn. If both started at zero, both gradients would stay zero forever.

blocks.md: **Initialization.** Hu et al. use a random Gaussian for A and zeros for B, so training starts exactly at the pretrained model. Hugging Face PEFT keeps B at zero by default and initializes A with a Kaiming-uniform draw; it also offers other schemes such as PiSSA and LoftQ.

**The alpha scaling.** The update is multiplied by $\alpha / r$, where $\alpha$ is a constant. Hu et al. explain that with Adam, tuning $\alpha$ is roughly like tuning the learning rate, so they set $\alpha$ to the first $r$ they try and leave it; the scaling reduces how much other hyperparameters need retuning when $r$ changes. In PEFT, `lora_alpha` and `r` both default to 8, and `use_rslora=True` switches the scale to $\alpha / \sqrt{r}$ (rank-stabilized LoRA).
LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.
LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r(d+k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

blocks.question: A colleague initializes both A and B to zero to be extra safe. What happens during training?
options: Training proceeds normally but more slowly
A learns first, then B
The update stays exactly zero, because each matrix's gradient is multiplied by the other matrix
The model diverges because the scale alpha/r is applied to zeros
blocks.explain: The gradient for B contains Ax and the gradient for A contains B. With both at zero, both gradients are zero at every step, so nothing ever changes. That is why one of the two must be random.

blocks.question: You change r from 8 to 16 but keep lora_alpha = 16. Compared with r = 8 and alpha = 16, what happens to the multiplier alpha/r?
options: It doubles from 1 to 2
It halves from 2 to 1
It stays 2, because PEFT rescales alpha automatically
It becomes alpha divided by the square root of r by default
blocks.explain: alpha/r goes from 16/8 = 2 to 16/16 = 1. With the default scaling the multiplier depends on r; only use_rslora=True switches to alpha/sqrt(r). Many recipes set alpha proportional to r (for example alpha = 2r) to keep the multiplier constant.

lessons.title: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference

blocks.md: Per adapted matrix of shape $d \times k$, LoRA trains $r(d+k)$ numbers. A 4096 by 4096 attention projection has 16,777,216 weights; a rank-8 adapter on it has $8 \times 8192 = 65{,}536$, which is 0.39%. The fraction is $r(d+k)/(dk)$, so it grows linearly with $r$.

A real model has many matrices. The script below counts them for a model with Llama-2-7B's shape (hidden size 4096, MLP size 11008, 32 layers, the defaults of Hugging Face's `LlamaConfig`). Each layer has four attention projections (query, key, value, output) and three MLP projections (gate, up, down).

blocks.code:
d, ff, L, vocab = 4096, 11008, 32, 32000   # Llama-2-7B shape
shapes = {"q": (d, d), "k": (d, d), "v": (d, d), "o": (d, d),
          "gate": (d, ff), "up": (d, ff), "down": (ff, d)}

def lora_params(r, modules):
    return L * sum(r * (shapes[m][0] + shapes[m][1]) for m in modules)

linear = L * sum(a * b for a, b in shapes.values())
total = linear + 2 * vocab * d + (2 * L + 1) * d  # + embed, head, norms

print(total)                                 # 6738415616
print(lora_params(8, ["q", "v"]))            # 4194304  (0.062%)
print(lora_params(16, shapes))               # 39976960 (0.593%)
print(lora_params(256, shapes))              # 639631360 (9.49%)
blocks.caption: Exact counts. Adapting only Wq and Wv at r = 8 trains 4.2M numbers; all seven linear layers at r = 16 trains 40M, still under 0.6% of the model.

blocks.title: Trainable share of a 7B model versus LoRA rank

scenes.caption: Both lines are straight on log axes because the count is linear in r. The LoRA paper's GPT-3 runs mostly used r = 1 to 8 on attention matrices only (Wq and Wv, or all four at r = 2), the bottom-left corner.

Targeting every linear layer costs about 4.8 times more per unit of rank. Even r = 256 on everything stays under 10% of the parameters, which is the setting Biderman et al. needed for hard code tasks (lesson 5).

blocks.md: Which matrices should get adapters? Hu et al. fixed a budget of about 18M parameters on GPT-3 175B (96 layers, $d = 12{,}288$) and spent it different ways. Spreading a small rank over Wq and Wv beat putting a bigger rank on one matrix. In a second table, rank 1 on Wq and Wv already scored 73.4 on WikiSQL, close to the best runs.

blocks.title: GPT-3 WikiSQL accuracy at a fixed 18M-parameter budget (Table 5)

scenes.caption: Single matrices: Wq or Wk alone are clearly worse (about 70) than Wv or Wo (about 73). Results vary by about 0.5 points across seeds.
Same budget split over more matrices: Wq with Wv at rank 4, or all four at rank 2, reach 73.7. Covering more matrices beats more rank in one.

blocks.md: Later work on harder tasks pushed further. The QLoRA authors could not match full fine-tuning of LLaMA 7B with adapters on Wq and Wv only; they needed LoRA on **all linear layers**, and found the rank mattered less than how many layers were adapted. Biderman et al. (2024) found most of the gain comes from the MLP modules. PEFT exposes this as `target_modules="all-linear"`.

**Merging.** Because the update is linear, after training you can compute $W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ once and serve that single matrix. The model then has exactly the original architecture and cost, so LoRA adds **zero inference latency** by construction. To switch tasks, subtract $BA$ and add another adapter's $B'A'$. PEFT does the merge with `merge_and_unload()`.

Earlier **adapter layers** (Houlsby et al. 2019) insert small extra layers into each block. They have few parameters, but they run in sequence after the layers they modify, which hurts when the batch is small and the GPU is mostly waiting on depth. Hu et al. measured this on GPT-2 medium.

blocks.title: GPT-2 medium forward latency, batch 1, 128 tokens (LoRA Table 1)

scenes.caption: A merged LoRA model is an ordinary model: 19.8 ms. Adapter variants add 20.7% and 30.3% at batch size 1, measured on a Quadro RTX8000. At batch 32 and 512 tokens the gap shrinks to 2 to 3%.

blocks.md: Storage follows the same arithmetic. The LoRA paper's GPT-3 adapter (r = 4 on Wq and Wv) is about 35 MB, so 100 task variants cost 350 GB + 100 x 35 MB, about 354 GB, instead of 100 x 350 GB = 35 TB.

Merging has a price: a merged model serves one adapter. Hu et al. note it is not straightforward to batch requests for *different* adapters in one forward pass once A and B are folded into W. Serving many adapters at once needs the unmerged form, which is the subject of the multi-LoRA serving course.

blocks.question: You add a rank-8 LoRA to one MLP up-projection of shape 4096 by 11008. How many trainable parameters does that adapter have?
blocks.explain: r(d + k) = 8 x (4096 + 11008) = 8 x 15104 = 120,832. 65,536 would be a square 4096 matrix, and 45,088,768 is the full matrix itself.

blocks.question: A latency-critical product serves one fine-tuned variant at batch size 1. Which deployment of a trained LoRA adds no per-token cost over the base model?
options: Merge W0 + (alpha/r)BA into one matrix before serving
Keep A and B separate and compute W0x + BAx on every token
Convert the LoRA into Houlsby adapter layers
Quantize B to 4 bits
blocks.explain: Once merged, the network has exactly the original shapes, so its cost is the base model's cost. Keeping the factors separate adds two small matmuls per adapted layer, and adapter layers add sequential depth, which Table 1 shows costs 20 to 30% at batch 1.

lessons.title: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model

blocks.md: LoRA removes gradients and optimizer state for the frozen weights, but the frozen weights still sit in GPU memory in 16 bits. For a 65B model that alone is about 130 GB. Dettmers et al. (2023) report that regular 16-bit fine-tuning of LLaMA 65B needs more than 780 GB of GPU memory, while **QLoRA** fine-tunes it on a single 48 GB GPU with no loss against 16-bit fine-tuning on their benchmarks.

The idea: store the frozen base model in 4 bits, keep LoRA adapters in 16-bit BFloat16, and backpropagate through the quantized weights into the adapters. Three pieces make this work: the **NF4** data type, **double quantization**, and **paged optimizers**.

**Block-wise quantization** first. Split a weight tensor into blocks (QLoRA uses 64 weights per block). Divide each block by its absolute maximum so values land in $[-1, 1]$, then round each to the nearest of 16 allowed values (4 bits). Store the 4-bit index plus one scale constant per block. Small blocks keep one outlier from wasting the grid for all other weights.

**4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)** picks those 16 values carefully. Pretrained weights are roughly zero-centered normal, so NF4 places its levels at quantiles of a standard normal distribution, rescaled to $[-1, 1]$: each level then receives about the same number of weights. The construction is made slightly asymmetric so that 0 is exactly representable (useful for padding and zero values).

blocks.title: Quantizing one block to NF4 (toy block of 8 weights)

scenes.caption: The 16 NF4 levels from the QLoRA paper's appendix, rounded. They are dense near 0, where most normally distributed weights are, and sparse near the ends.
A block of 8 weights (real QLoRA blocks hold 64). The largest magnitude is 0.064, so the block's scale constant is c = 0.064.
Divide by c: every value now lies in [-1, 1], and the absmax weight maps exactly to -1.
Round each to the nearest NF4 level and store its index (0 to 15). For example 0.734 is closest to level 14 (0.72) and 0.188 to level 9 (0.16). These indices are the 4-bit weights.

Dequantize: level value times c. Mean absolute error is 0.00127. A uniform 15-level 4-bit grid on the same block gives 0.00211 (one toy block; the paper's evidence is the perplexity and accuracy tables).

blocks.md: **Double quantization.** One fp32 constant per 64 weights costs $32/64 = 0.5$ extra bits per parameter. QLoRA quantizes those constants too: they become 8-bit floats in blocks of 256, each block with its own fp32 constant.

blocks.caption: Saving: about 0.373 bits per parameter, which the paper puts at about 3 GB for a 65B model.

blocks.md: **Paged optimizers** handle memory spikes. They allocate the optimizer state in NVIDIA unified memory, which pages it to CPU RAM automatically when the GPU runs out (for example on a long-sequence batch with gradient checkpointing) and pages it back when the optimizer step needs it.

scenes.caption: Storage type: the frozen weight lives in NF4 with double-quantized block constants. This is where the memory saving comes from.
Compute type: on every use the weight is dequantized to BF16 and multiplied in 16-bit. 4-bit is only how it is stored.
The LoRA path runs alongside in BF16 and the two are summed (QLoRA Eq. 5).
Backward: gradients flow through the dequantized W to reach the input, but only L1 and L2 get weight gradients and optimizer state, which is paged to CPU if the GPU fills up.

blocks.title: Estimated memory for a 7B model (weights and optimizer only)

scenes.caption: Script estimates for the 6.74B model: full fine-tuning 107.8 GB; LoRA keeps a 13.5 GB BF16 base plus 0.64 GB for 40M adapter parameters with their gradients and Adam state; QLoRA shrinks the base to about 3.9 GB (embeddings and output head left in BF16).
Simplified: activations are not counted, and the QLoRA paper reports a measured 5,048 MB for its 4-bit 7B base. Treat these bars as lower bounds that show the ratios.

blocks.md: Does 4-bit storage hurt quality? In the paper's Table 4, LLaMA 7B to 65B fine-tuned with NF4 plus double quantization averaged 53.1 on 5-shot MMLU against 53.0 for 16-bit LoRA, while plain 4-bit floats (FP4) averaged 52.2. On GLUE and Super-NaturalInstructions, 4-bit QLoRA also matched 16-bit full fine-tuning of RoBERTa and T5.

QLoRA separates a storage type (NF4, 4 bits) from a compute type (BF16). Only the adapters are trained, so quantization error in the frozen base can be compensated by the adapters, and memory drops by about 4x versus a 16-bit base.

blocks.question: Double quantization saves about 0.373 bits per parameter. Roughly how much is that for a 65B model?
options: About 0.3 GB
About 24 GB
About 30 GB
About 3 GB
blocks.explain: 65e9 parameters x 0.373 bits = 2.42e10 bits, divided by 8 is about 3.0e9 bytes, about 3 GB, matching the paper's figure. Small per parameter, but enough to decide whether a 65B model fits on a 48 GB card.

blocks.question: Why does NF4 put more of its 16 levels near zero than a uniform 4-bit integer grid does?
options: Because pretrained weights are roughly normal, so equal-probability bins are dense where most weights lie
Because zero-valued weights are pruned and need no levels
Because the GPU can only multiply by values close to zero
Because the adapters only change weights near zero
blocks.explain: NF4 is a quantile quantizer for a normal distribution: each of the 16 bins holds about the same share of weights. Since most weights cluster near zero, the levels cluster there too, which lowers average rounding error for normally distributed data.

blocks.question: During QLoRA training, which statement about the 4-bit base weights is true?
options: They are updated in 4 bits by a special optimizer
They are converted to BF16 once at load time and kept that way
They are dequantized to BF16 for each matmul, gradients pass through them, but they are never updated
They are skipped in the backward pass, so earlier layers get no gradient
blocks.explain: The NF4 weights are the storage format. Each use dequantizes them to BF16 for the forward and backward matmuls, so gradients reach earlier adapters, but no weight gradient or optimizer state is kept for the frozen base.

lessons.title: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short

blocks.md: LoRA is one member of a family called **parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)**: freeze the pretrained model and train a small add-on. The methods differ in *where* the add-on goes, which decides whether it costs inference time or context length.

- **Adapters** (Houlsby et al. 2019): small bottleneck layers (down-project, nonlinearity, up-project) inserted after attention and after the MLP in each block. On GLUE they came within 0.4% of full fine-tuning while adding 3.6% parameters per task, but they add sequential depth at inference.
- **Prefix tuning** (Li and Liang 2021): learn continuous vectors that act like extra *virtual tokens* at every layer, which real tokens attend to. About 0.1% of parameters on their generation tasks.
- **Prompt tuning** (Lester et al. 2021): learn only a soft prompt at the input embedding. On T5 it closes the gap with full model tuning as models pass billions of parameters.

- **(IA)3** (Liu et al. 2022): learn three vectors that rescale keys, values and the MLP's inner activations by element-wise multiplication. Only three vectors per layer, and since it is a rescaling, it can be folded into the weights.
- **DoRA** (Liu et al. 2024): split each pretrained weight into a per-column **magnitude** and a unit-norm **direction**, train the magnitude vector directly and the direction with a LoRA update. It merges back into one matrix, so it adds no inference overhead.

blocks.caption: DoRA (Liu et al. 2024, Eq. 5). The norm is taken column by column; m is a trainable vector of column magnitudes.

scenes.caption: The frozen backbone: embeddings, then attention and MLP in every layer.
Input-side methods add no weights to the layers, but every virtual token takes sequence length. On GPT-3, Hu et al. saw quality drop past 256 prefix-embedding tokens or 32 prefix-layer tokens.
Adapters add new layers on the main path. That costs extra sequential compute at inference unless the model is restructured.
LoRA, DoRA and (IA)3 modify existing weights in ways that can be merged after training, so the served model has the original shape and cost.

blocks.md: Is LoRA as good as full fine-tuning? Hu et al. and Dettmers et al. found it matched on their benchmarks. Biderman et al. (2024, "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less") tested harder settings with Llama-2-7B: code and math, both **instruction fine-tuning** (about 100K prompt-response pairs) and **continued pretraining** (billions of raw tokens).

blocks.title: Llama-2-7B on Magicoder code instructions, epoch 4 (Tables S5, S6)

scenes.caption: Learning: HumanEval pass@1. Ranks 16 and 64 (0.358, 0.417) trail full fine-tuning (0.470 here, 0.497 at its best epoch). Only r = 256 catches up (0.498).
Forgetting: average of HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge and Winogrande, higher means less forgotten. Full fine-tuning has dropped to 0.512 while every LoRA rank stays at 0.63 or above.

blocks.md: In continued pretraining on code the gap never closed: the best LoRA (r = 256) peaked at HumanEval 0.224 after 20B tokens, roughly what full fine-tuning reached after 4B tokens, while full fine-tuning peaked at 0.263. Their SVD analysis suggests why: the weight change that full fine-tuning learns has rank 10 to 100 times higher than typical LoRA ranks, and the rank keeps growing with more data.

The flip side is **catastrophic forgetting**, the loss of earlier abilities when a model is trained on a new domain. LoRA forgot less than full fine-tuning in every code setting, and more effectively than dropout or weight decay. More rank and more training made LoRA learn more and forget more.

Practical guidance from these papers:
- Use LoRA for instruction tuning and narrow tasks; prefer full fine-tuning for continued pretraining on a new domain.
- Target all linear layers, not just Wq and Wv.
- For hard domains like code, try high ranks (Biderman et al. used 256) with alpha = 2r.
- LoRA's best learning rate is often about 10x higher than full fine-tuning's (they swept 1e-5 to 5e-4).

Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

blocks.question: A team wants to teach Llama-2-7B a new programming language by training on 20B tokens of raw source code, and to keep its English skills. What does the evidence suggest?
options: LoRA at r = 16 will match full fine-tuning and forget nothing
Full fine-tuning will likely learn the domain better, while LoRA preserves more of the base skills; pick based on which matters more
Prompt tuning is the best choice because it has the fewest parameters
Rank does not matter in continued pretraining
blocks.explain: In Biderman et al.'s continued pretraining runs, full fine-tuning outperformed every LoRA rank on the target domain, and LoRA forgot less. That is a real tradeoff, not a free lunch, and rank clearly ordered LoRA's results.

blocks.question: Which PEFT method from this lesson consumes part of the model's context window?
options: LoRA
(IA)3
DoRA
Prefix and prompt tuning
blocks.explain: Prompt and prefix tuning add virtual tokens that sit in the sequence, so they take positions that real input could have used. LoRA, DoRA and (IA)3 change weights or rescale activations and can be merged into the model.

blocks.question: Your LoRA r = 16 on attention only underperforms full fine-tuning on a code instruction set. Which change is most supported by the evidence in this course?
options: Lower the learning rate by 10x
Switch to adapting only Wq
Target all linear layers including the MLP and raise the rank
Initialize B randomly instead of to zero
blocks.explain: QLoRA needed all linear layers to match full fine-tuning, and Biderman et al. found MLP modules drive most gains and that code needs high ranks. Their recommendation was a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, not lower.
